El infinito en un junco: So many people recommended it, and when Carissa Véliz called it a marvel in Prophecy, I had to read it. I'm still at the beginning, but I love how naturally Vallejo tells the history of books.
Good Strategy Bad Strategy: I come back to this one a lot when working on product strategy. It makes me face the difficult questions I'd rather avoid and think more clearly about what we're actually trying to achieve. I'd recommend it to anyone in product.
Music Law in the Digital Age: One of the books I use most in my licensing work, whether I'm reviewing contracts or building data tools. If you're working on a digital product that uses music, it's well worth having around.
Inspired: This one always gets me excited about product discovery again. Especially useful if, like me, you came into product from another field. It gives us a common language to work with.
Never Split the Difference: I use a lot of what I learned here in my licensing negotiations. It gives you a better way to think about concessions, approach difficult conversations and work towards an agreement together. Useful well beyond work.
Prophecy: I think about this book a lot. It made me more aware of the assumptions behind the algorithms and predictions we live with, and more careful about how I interpret statistical results. I'd recommend it to anyone.
La perra: I read it during a humid summer and could almost feel the Pacific coast of Chocó around me. I love how deeply Pilar Quintana gets into her characters. I was completely absorbed.
Los abismos: I read it while travelling around Colombia. You can almost feel the heat of Cali. I loved how she writes about imperfect mothers. She's one of my favourite Colombian writers.
Lo que no tiene nombre: I read it in one sitting on a Sunday afternoon and barely noticed the time. I admire how deeply and calmly Piedad writes about something so painful. I'd recommend it to anyone going through grief.
Donde cantan las ballenas: The ending still gets to me. It took me years to finish it because I had to wait until I felt ready. I love seeing our Latin American magical realism through the eyes of a little girl.
Mujeres que corren con los lobos: It helped me through a very difficult time. I love how it explores feminine archetypes. I think every woman should read it. It's our bible.
La clase de griego: I read it in a couple of days and didn't want to put it down. I loved the way Han Kang describes sensations, and especially his letters. More about atmosphere than plot, which I really enjoy.
La vegetariana: I read it over a couple of nights. It made me think a lot about how society sees women's bodies, how much of ourselves belongs to us, and what it means to be free.
La ridícula idea de no volver a verte: I never thought a book about Marie Curie would make me cry. I love Rosa Montero's voice. I read it slowly over a couple of weeks because I didn't want it to end. A lovely book for anyone trying to make sense of grief.
